title: The science of browning food
examples: What is the difference between browning from Maillard and caramelisation?
Does the pH level affect how fast these reactions happen?
Can I control the browning process when I bake bread?

explain.say: Today we are learning about how food browns when we cook it.
First we look at the Maillard reaction, which needs amino acids and sugars.
A simple example is when we cook bread or toast it lightly.
Next we study caramelisation, which only involves heating sugars alone.
A clear example is when you make caramel for a dessert topping.
In real life, think about frying bacon in a pan.

faq.q: What is the main difference between the two reactions?
faq.a: The Maillard reaction needs both amino acids and sugars to happen. Caramelisation only requires heating sugars by themselves.
asks: Do I need protein for caramel?
Which reaction needs more than just sugar?

faq.q: Does the temperature affect which reaction happens?
faq.a: Yes, both reactions are sped up by heat. However, caramelisation often requires very high, sustained heat.
asks: Is heat the only thing that matters?
At what temperature do these reactions start?

faq.q: Can I stop the browning process if I don't want it?
faq.a: You can slow it down by cooling the food or by adding an acid, which can inhibit the reactions.
asks: How do I keep food from turning brown?
Is there a way to prevent browning?

faq.q: Do these reactions create all the flavor in cooked food?
faq.a: No, they create many of the wonderful savory and sweet flavors, but other compounds also contribute to the overall taste.
asks: Is flavor only from these two reactions?
What else gives food its taste?

faq.q: What happens if I cook something too long?
faq.a: If you cook it too long, the reactions continue, and the food might become bitter or burnt.
asks: Can I overcook food using these principles?
What is the danger of prolonged cooking?

facts: The Maillard reaction gives food its savory, 'cooked' flavor.
Caramelisation is the thermal decomposition of sugars.
Both reactions are accelerated by higher temperatures.
The reaction products are responsible for the brown color.

quiz.say: When you bake cookies that brown beautifully, which reaction is primarily responsible for the color?
quiz.why: Cookies contain both sugars and proteins from eggs and flour, so both reactions occur, but the Maillard reaction is key for the complex browning.

wrong.0: This is wrong because boiling is a process, not a specific chemical reaction causing browning.
wrong.2: This is wrong because caramelisation only involves sugars, but cookies also contain proteins.
wrong.3: This is wrong because oxidation usually happens slowly when exposed to air, not rapidly from high heat.

quiz.say: If you heat pure sugar until it turns a deep amber color, what process is happening?
quiz.why: Heating sugar alone causes it to break down into new compounds, which is the definition of caramelisation.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the Maillard reaction requires amino acids to take place.
wrong.2: This is wrong because hydrolysis involves breaking bonds using water, not just heat.
wrong.3: This is wrong because evaporation is the change of liquid to gas, not a chemical change causing color.

quiz.say: Which condition is absolutely necessary for the Maillard reaction to occur?
quiz.why: The Maillard reaction is defined by the interaction between amino acids (from proteins) and reducing sugars.

wrong.0: This is wrong because if only sugars are present, only caramelisation can happen.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the reaction requires heat and the presence of reactants, not just a lack of air.
wrong.3: This is wrong because while heat speeds it up, the reactants (amino acids and sugars) must also be present.
